description: Primary and secondary food processing, how they affect nutrition and flavour, plus fortification and modified foods.
content_html:
Food Processing: From Raw Ingredient to Finished Product

Most food we eat has been processed in some way before it reaches our kitchens. Processing transforms raw ingredients into safe, convenient and long-lasting food products. Understanding the difference between primary and secondary processing — and how each stage affects the nutritional and sensory properties of food — is essential knowledge for this qualification.

Primary Processing

Primary processing is the first stage — converting raw plant or animal material into a basic ingredient. It includes:

  • Growing and harvesting: wheat is planted, grows and is harvested by combine harvester. The grain is then cleaned and dried to a safe moisture level.
  • Milling of wheat to flour: harvested wheat grains are milled (ground) between rollers to produce flour. Wholemeal flour retains all parts of the grain — bran, germ and endosperm. White flour removes the bran and germ, giving a lighter flour with a longer shelf life but reduced fibre, vitamins and minerals.
  • Heat treatment of milk: raw milk from cows undergoes heat treatment to destroy harmful bacteria. Pasteurisation heats milk to 72°C for 15 seconds. UHT (ultra-heat treatment) heats milk to at least 135°C for one to two seconds, giving a shelf life of several months without refrigeration. Sterilised milk is heated to above 100°C in sealed bottles. Micro-filtered milk uses physical filtration rather than heat to remove bacteria.
  • Fishing and rearing: catching fish from the sea or harvesting from aquaculture farms; slaughtering and dressing meat to produce cuts ready for secondary processing.
Key Fact

Primary processing converts a raw material into a basic ingredient. Examples: milling wheat into flour; pasteurising raw milk; harvesting fish; cleaning and drying grain after harvest.

Secondary Processing

Secondary processing takes a primary processed ingredient and turns it into a recognisable food product. Examples include:

  • Flour into bread and pasta: flour is mixed with water (and yeast for bread) to form a dough. In breadmaking, yeast ferments sugars to produce carbon dioxide, which causes the dough to rise. Baking in the oven then sets the gluten network and browns the crust through dextrinisation. In pasta-making, semolina flour is extruded into shapes and dried.
  • Milk into cheese and yoghurt: pasteurised milk is acidified with bacterial cultures. For yoghurt, Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid, thickening the milk and giving a tangy flavour. For cheese, rennet is added to coagulate the milk proteins, forming curds which are pressed, salted and matured. Blue cheese involves the growth of specific moulds to produce characteristic flavour and appearance.
  • Fruit into jams: fruit is cooked with sugar. High temperatures destroy enzymes and most bacteria, preserving the jam. The pectin naturally present in some fruits gels with sugar to create the characteristic set. Strawberry jam made from British summer strawberries is a classic example of secondary processing transforming a seasonal fruit into a product that lasts all year.

A common exam error is to describe the whole production chain under “primary processing”. Primary processing turns a raw biological material into a basic ingredient: wheat → flour; raw milk → pasteurised milk. Secondary processing takes that ingredient and makes a food product: flour → bread; pasteurised milk → yoghurt. The test: can you eat the primary processed ingredient straight away? Flour and pasteurised milk are usable ingredients but are not finished food products. If the answer is “yes, this is a ready-to-eat or ready-to-cook product”, you are in secondary processing territory.

How Processing Affects Nutritional and Sensory Properties

Processing inevitably changes food. Some changes improve safety; others reduce nutritional value. Loss of vitamins through heating: water-soluble vitamins (B group vitamins and vitamin C) are vulnerable to heat and leach into cooking water. Blanching, pasteurisation and UHT processing all destroy some B vitamins. UHT milk loses more B vitamins and has a slightly cooked flavour compared with pasteurised milk because of the higher processing temperature. Milling white flour removes the bran and germ, stripping much of the thiamin (B1), niacin (B3), iron and fibre from the grain. Drying concentrates flavour and extends shelf life but similarly destroys heat-sensitive vitamins. Dried fruit has more sugar per gram and less vitamin C than fresh.

Key Fact

Water-soluble vitamins — including B group vitamins and vitamin C — are destroyed by heat. UHT milk is heated to a higher temperature than pasteurised milk, so it loses more B vitamins and has a slightly cooked taste. Milling white flour also strips out thiamin, niacin, iron and fibre.

Technological Developments: Fortification

Fortification is a technological response to nutrient loss. In the UK, it is a legal requirement to add thiamin (B1), niacin (B3), calcium and iron back into white flour to replace what is removed during milling. Breakfast cereals are often additionally fortified with folic acid and iron — partly because folic acid is important in reducing the risk of neural tube defects in early pregnancy, and many women consume cereal daily. Margarine and low-fat spreads are usually fortified with vitamins A and D on a voluntary basis, because these fat-soluble vitamins are naturally present in butter but lost when dairy fat is replaced with vegetable oil.

Fortification adds nutrients that were lost in processing or are lacking in the population’s diet — it is essentially restoration or supplementation. Modification (as in modified foods) changes the food’s functional properties or composition to deliver a specific health benefit, often through the addition of bioactive compounds not naturally present in significant amounts. Cholesterol-lowering spreads are modified: plant sterols (phytosterols) or stanols are added at concentrations far higher than naturally occur in food because at those levels they block cholesterol absorption in the gut. In your exam, use the correct term for the correct type of technological development: fortification = adding lost or missing vitamins/minerals; modification = adding bioactive ingredients to change a physiological function.

Technological Developments: Cholesterol-Lowering Spreads and Modified Foods

Cholesterol-lowering spreads are a well-established example of modified foods. They contain plant sterols or stanols, which are structurally similar to cholesterol. When consumed regularly, they compete with dietary cholesterol for absorption in the small intestine, reducing the amount of LDL (“bad”) cholesterol that enters the bloodstream. Clinical evidence supports a reduction of LDL cholesterol by approximately 10–15% when these spreads are consumed daily as directed. However, there are limitations: they are more expensive than standard spreads, the cholesterol-lowering effect requires daily consistent use, and they are not suitable for pregnant women or children without medical guidance.

Other examples of modified foods include probiotic yoghurts (containing live bacterial cultures claimed to support gut health), omega-3 enriched eggs (from hens fed flaxseed or fish oil) and high-fibre breads with added inulin. The positive and negative aspects of food additives — including colourings, emulsifiers, stabilisers, flavourings and preservatives — are also part of this topic. Preservatives such as sulphur dioxide (in dried fruit) and sodium nitrate (in processed meat) extend shelf life significantly but some consumers prefer to avoid them.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about fortification, students often confuse why fortification is used (the public health reason) with what is added (the specific nutrients). A top-band answer covers both: the processing reason (milling removes thiamin and niacin from white flour) and the public health outcome (deficiency in thiamin causes beriberi; widespread fortification ensures the general population meets its requirements). Use the words “because” and “this means that” to chain your reasoning. For a 9-mark Analyse question on modified foods, identify the specific mechanism (plant sterols blocking cholesterol absorption), the evidence of benefit (LDL reduction of 10–15%), and the limitations (cost, requirement for daily use, unsuitable groups) — analysing the relationship between all three earns Mastering marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary processing converts raw materials into basic ingredients (e.g. wheat → flour, raw milk → pasteurised milk); secondary processing transforms those ingredients into food products (flour → bread, milk → yoghurt).
  • Processing can destroy water-soluble vitamins (B group, vitamin C) through heat, and milling white flour removes thiamin, niacin, iron and fibre from wheat.
  • Fortification restores or adds missing nutrients (thiamin, niacin, calcium and iron in white flour; folic acid and iron in breakfast cereals; vitamins A and D in margarine); cholesterol-lowering spreads are modified foods where plant sterols reduce LDL cholesterol absorption when consumed daily.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of primary processing?
A. Turning flour into bread dough
B. Converting milk into yoghurt using bacterial cultures
C. Milling harvested wheat grain into flour
D. Cooking fruit with sugar to produce jam
State two nutrients that are legally required to be added back to white flour during fortification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two from: thiamin (B1); niacin (B3); calcium; iron. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how UHT processing of milk differs from pasteurisation and explain one effect this difference has on the milk's nutritional or sensory properties.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the temperature/time difference: UHT heats milk to at least 135°C for 1–2 seconds compared with pasteurisation at 72°C for 15 seconds (1). 1 mark for the consequence: UHT causes greater destruction of heat-sensitive B vitamins (1). 1 mark for the sensory or practical effect: UHT has a slightly cooked or caramelised flavour compared with pasteurised milk, and does not require refrigeration until opened (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Tariq is a 45-year-old man who has been told by his GP to reduce his LDL cholesterol. His dietitian suggests switching to a cholesterol-lowering spread. Explain how cholesterol-lowering spreads work and whether they are a reliable solution for Tariq.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Mechanism (2): cholesterol-lowering spreads contain plant sterols or stanols which are structurally similar to cholesterol (1); they compete with dietary cholesterol for absorption in the small intestine, reducing the amount that enters the bloodstream (1). Reliability evaluation (2): evidence supports a reduction in LDL cholesterol of approximately 10–15% with daily consistent use (1); however, the effect requires daily use and the spread is more expensive than standard alternatives, which means Tariq needs to use it every day to see benefit (1). Two developed explanations for full marks.

practice_questions.text: A breakfast cereal manufacturer is updating its product range. One new cereal is fortified with folic acid and iron; another is modified to include added plant sterols. Evaluate the health benefits and limitations of using fortification and modification as strategies to improve public health through food.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Distinguishes clearly between fortification (restoring lost/absent nutrients for a population) and modification (adding bioactive compounds to produce a physiological change). Health benefits of fortification developed: folic acid reduces risk of neural tube defects in early pregnancy; iron fortification addresses widespread iron-deficiency anaemia, particularly in young women and adolescents; calcium and B vitamins in flour support bone health and nervous system function across the population. Limitations of fortification: does not help individuals with specific deficiencies needing medical intervention; fortified food still needs to be consumed daily; over-fortification of some nutrients (e.g. fat-soluble vitamins A and D) could cause toxicity if multiple fortified products consumed. Health benefits of modification developed: plant sterols in spreads clinically proven to reduce LDL cholesterol by 10–15% with daily use, supporting cardiovascular health. Limitations of modification: requires daily consistent use; not suitable for pregnant women or children; higher cost limits accessibility; effect on some groups unproven; consumers may over-rely on modified foods rather than broader dietary change. Reaches a supported judgement: fortification is the more reliable public health tool because it benefits the whole population passively (e.g. white flour is in bread eaten daily by most people), whereas modified foods require specific conscious purchasing and daily compliance. Accurate and sustained use of terminology throughout. Judgement explicitly weighs the scale of benefit (whole-population vs individual daily users).

Secure (7–9): Addresses both fortification and modification with developed points for each. Benefits and limitations present for both. Reaches a judgement but the weighing of evidence is partial.

Developing (4–6): Identifies benefits and limitations of one or both strategies with some development. May be one-sided or descriptive. Judgement present but weakly supported.

Emerging (1–3): Basic identification of benefits. Little or no analysis of limitations. No judgement or judgement unsupported. May confuse fortification and modification.

practice_questions.text: Give one example of secondary processing that uses milk as its primary processed starting ingredient.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one correct example of secondary processing using milk: yoghurt; cheese (any variety); butter; cream; ice cream. Answer must name a product made from milk, not just describe a process.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes secondary processing?
options: Harvesting wheat and cleaning the grain
Pasteurising raw milk to kill harmful bacteria
Converting flour into bread dough and baking it
Milling wheat grain into white flour

knowledge_checks.q: Which vitamin is added to margarine and low-fat spreads in the UK to replace what is lost when dairy fat is replaced with vegetable oil?
Milling wheat to produce white flour removes the bran and germ, stripping out thiamin, niacin, iron and _____.
Cholesterol-lowering spreads contain plant _____, which block the absorption of dietary cholesterol in the small intestine.
Match each food product with the correct processing stage that produces it.
right: Secondary processing: flour fermented with yeast and baked
Primary processing: milk heated to 72°C for 15 seconds
Secondary processing: milk fermented with bacterial cultures
Primary processing: wheat grain milled between rollers

flashcard_questions.a: Converting a raw material into a basic ingredient, e.g. milling wheat into flour.
Transforming a primary processed ingredient into a finished food product, e.g. flour into bread.

flashcard_questions.q: What temperature does pasteurisation heat milk to, and for how long?
Why does UHT milk have a longer shelf life than pasteurised milk?
flashcard_questions.a: It is heated to at least 135°C, destroying more bacteria and allowing unopened storage without refrigeration.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two water-soluble vitamin groups are most vulnerable to heat during food processing?
flashcard_questions.a: B group vitamins and vitamin C.
Adding nutrients to food to replace those lost in processing or to boost nutritional content for public health.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four nutrients that must legally be added to white flour in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: Thiamin (B1), niacin (B3), calcium, iron — all four replaced to compensate for losses in milling.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is folic acid added to many breakfast cereals?
flashcard_questions.a: To reduce the risk of neural tube defects in early pregnancy, as many women eat cereal daily.

flashcard_questions.q: What vitamins must be added to margarine and low-fat spreads in the UK?
How do plant sterols in cholesterol-lowering spreads reduce LDL cholesterol?
flashcard_questions.a: They compete with dietary cholesterol for absorption in the small intestine, so less enters the bloodstream.

flashcard_questions.q: By approximately how much can cholesterol-lowering spreads reduce LDL cholesterol with daily use?
Give one limitation of cholesterol-lowering spreads as a health intervention.
flashcard_questions.a: They require daily consistent use, are more expensive than standard spreads, and are unsuitable for young children and pregnant women.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of bacteria is used to ferment milk into yoghurt?
flashcard_questions.a: Lactobacillus bacteria, which convert lactose into lactic acid.

glossary_terms.definition: The initial handling of raw food materials through activities such as rearing, growing, harvesting, fishing, cleaning and milling to produce a basic ingredient ready for further use.
The stage of food production that takes a primary processed ingredient and transforms it into a finished or semi-finished food product, such as turning flour into bread or milk into cheese.
A heat treatment that heats milk to 72°C for 15 seconds and then rapidly cools it, killing most harmful bacteria while preserving flavour.
A heat treatment that heats milk to at least 135°C for 1-2 seconds, producing a shelf-stable product that does not need refrigeration until opened.
The addition of nutrients to a food product, either to replace those lost during processing or to boost nutritional content above natural levels for a public health benefit.
Food products that have been technologically altered to deliver a specific health benefit, such as the addition of plant sterols to spreads to reduce LDL cholesterol absorption.
